fact: Motz, an infill maker, says how often infill needs replenishing depends on the infill type, how much use and foot traffic the area gets, the climate and weather, and the maintenance routine, and advises checking depth with an infill gauge once a year, or every six months in higher-use areas, rather than following a fixed timeline.
quote: The frequency depends on several factors, including the type of infill used, the area’s level of usage and foot traffic, the climate and weather conditions, and your overall maintenance routine. … Rather than adhering to an arbitrary timeline for infill replenishment, keep tabs on your turf system by checking for infill depth once a year (or as often as every six months in higher-use areas), using an infill gauge and your infill manufacturer’s depth guidelines.
source_label: The Motz Group, How Much Artificial Turf Infill Do I Need? (July 30, 2018)
notes: Section 'How Often Do I Need to Top Off or Replace My Artificial Turf Infill?'. Motz sells Envirofill and Safeshell; the page names it as a maker.

fact: Motz says to fix a few low spots by adding handfuls of infill in thin layers, because both too little and too much infill can cause matting and cost the turf cushioning and drainage, to brush it in afterwards, and to consult an expert when infill is extremely low throughout.
quote: If you only have a few low-infill areas, start by adding handfuls of infill directly into those spots. Apply a thin layer at a time to avoid overfilling, as both too little and too much infill can lead to matting and cosmetic issues, not to mention a loss of turf’s cushioning and drainage. After more infill is added, you can use your broom, Grandi Groom, or a small artificial grass brush to work it into the turf. If your infill is extremely low throughout, it’s a good idea to bring in or consult with an expert for any larger-scale infill replenishments or replacements.
source_label: The Motz Group, How Much Artificial Turf Infill Do I Need? (July 30, 2018)

fact: Motz measures infill depth from the base of the turf system to the top of the infill layer and tells owners to check the turf maker's guidelines for the infill type and quantity their turf calls for.
quote: What is your needed infill depth (measured from the base of the turf system to the top of the infill layer)? Does your specific turf type come with infill specifications? Always check the manufacturer’s guidelines for any unique requirements for infill type and quantity.
source_label: The Motz Group, How Much Artificial Turf Infill Do I Need? (July 30, 2018)

fact: Motz recommends 1.25 to 1.75 pounds per square foot of its walnut-shell infill, Safeshell, on landscape turf with a 1.5 to 1.75 inch pile, and says some organic infills migrate easily and need frequent top-offs.
quote: However, some organic infills can migrate easily and require frequent top-offs, making them higher maintenance than non-organic products. … With Safeshell infill used in landscaping applications with a turf pile height of 1½ – 1¾”, we recommend 1.25 to 1.75 pounds of infill per square foot.
source_label: The Motz Group, How Much Artificial Turf Infill Do I Need? (July 30, 2018)
notes: Motz contrasts other organic infills with its own walnut product, which it says does not float or break down; the page reports only the rate and the general migration point.

fact: In a 2021 post the same maker gives a rule of thumb of replenishing or replacing infill at least every 18 months, sooner if the yard shows it, says pet play areas may need topping off every three to six months, and suggests keeping a couple of bags of the same infill on hand.
quote: A good rule of thumb is to replenish or replace your synthetic turf infill at least every 18 months, but keep an eye on your yard to see if you need to do it sooner. … Consider having a couple of bags of your selected turf infill stored in your shed or garage at all times to replenish levels as needed. … In especially high-traffic areas, like pet play areas, you may need to top off your infill levels every three to six months.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Get Turf to Stand Up Tall When Flat (May 27, 2021)
notes: The 2018 post from the same maker says to check depth rather than follow an arbitrary timeline; the page presents both.

fact: Motz says installers often put too little infill into new turf, that infill settles and is displaced over time in high-traffic areas, that children and pets move it around, and that levels move more in regions with four seasons and lots of precipitation.
quote: Often, installers don’t add enough infill to brand-new turf systems. … Infill levels naturally settle and material can be displaced over time, especially in highly trafficked areas of your yard. Have kids or pets? Small running feet and paws are known to move infill around. You’re also more likely to see movement in your infill levels if you live in a region with four seasons and lots of precipitation, too.
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Get Turf to Stand Up Tall When Flat (May 27, 2021)

fact: Motz says blades pressed down lightly should spring straight back, that spots which stay flat or matted may need more infill, and that too much infill can impede drainage and leave the surface uncomfortably hard.
quote: The turf fibers should feel relatively stiff and resilient, and if you press down lightly on them, the blades should bounce back up immediately when you release pressure. If you do this and are left with flat artificial grass in that spot, or if some areas of your turf system still appear flat or matted, more infill may be needed. … (FYI: Too much infill can also impede drainage and counteract the cushioning effect that synthetic turf infill is meant to provide, leaving you with an uncomfortably hard or even unsafe turf surface.)
source_label: The Motz Group, How to Get Turf to Stand Up Tall When Flat (May 27, 2021)

fact: Motz says its coated sand works best alone: it can be used to top off a different infill already in the turf, but performance may not match, and the maker recommends removing and replacing the old infill instead.
quote: Envirofill is a homogenous infill that works best alone. However, if infill replacement is not an option for you, your current infill can be topped off with Envirofill. … In this situation, performance may not be the same as a sole Envirofill installation. Our recommendation for best performance and longevity is to remove and replace your infill with Envirofill instead of topping off.
source_label: The Motz Group, Synthetic Turf Infill FAQ

fact: Motz sells its Envirofill coated sand in 50-pound bags and its Safeshell walnut infill in 25-pound bags.
quote: Envirofill is sold in 50lb bags and Safeshell is sold in 25lb bags
source_label: The Motz Group, Synthetic Turf Infill FAQ
notes: The FAQ answer has no closing period.

fact: Motz says the turf should be completely dry before infill goes down so it does not clump on the fibers, advises checking before winter that there is enough infill spread evenly to keep the turf stable, and says crumb rubber disperses easily when snow is removed.
quote: Ensure that the drainage system is free from blockages and that there is enough infill distributed evenly across the turf to keep it stable. … crumb rubber loosens up and disperses easily with snow removal. … Just make sure that the artificial turf is completely dry before laying down infill, so it doesn’t clump on turf fibers.
source_label: The Motz Group, The Ultimate Guide to Protecting Your Home's Artificial Turf in the Winter (Jan. 25, 2024)
notes: The dry-turf sentence answers whether turf can be installed in winter; the principle is the same for a top-up.

fact: Motz's Envirofill installation chart pairs a 1 to 1.25 inch pet or playground pile with 3/8 to 1/2 inch of infill at 1.5 to 2.5 pounds per square foot, a 1.5 to 1.75 inch landscape pile with 1/2 to 3/4 inch at 2.5 to 3.5 pounds, and a 1.875 to 2.25 inch landscape pile with 3/4 to 1 inch at 3.5 to 4.5 pounds, allows a variance of about 1/4 inch or 0.5 pound, and ends with checking the depth with an infill measuring device.
quote: 10. Finally, use an infill measuring device to confirm proper recommended depth. … Please note that a variance of approx. ¼” (6mm) or .5lbs (.23kg) may be acceptable dependent upon the application type. … 12/20 or 16/30 1-1¼” (25-32mm) Pet/Playground ⅜” – ½” (10-13mm) 1.5-2.5lbs (7.32-12.21kg/m2) 12/20 or 16/30 1½-1 ¾” (38-44mm) Landscape ½” – ¾” (13-19mm) 2.5-3.5lbs (12.21-17.09kg/m2) 12/20 or 16/30 1⅞”-2 ¼” (48-57mm) Landscape ¾” – 1” (19-25mm) 3.5-4.5lbs (17.09-21.97kg/m2)
source_label: The Motz Group, Envirofill Installation Guidelines: Landscape & Recreational Applications (PDF)
notes: The chart rows are quoted in reading order (size, pile height, turf spec, depth, pounds per square foot). Fractions 1¼, 1½, 1¾, 1⅞ and 2¼ inch are written 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 1.875 and 2.25 in the fact.

fact: Arithmetic on Motz's chart, not the maker's statement: on 1.5 to 1.75 inch landscape turf the chart's 1/2 to 3/4 inch depth range spans 2.5 to 3.5 pounds per square foot, so bringing a 150-square-foot path from the bottom of that range to its middle takes about 0.5 pound per square foot, roughly 75 pounds, or two 50-pound bags.
source_label: The Motz Group, Envirofill Installation Guidelines: Landscape & Recreational Applications (PDF), landscape row
notes: Worked example for the guide. Linear reading of one chart row: the 1/4 inch between the ends of the depth range spans 1 lb/sq ft, so the midpoint is 0.5 lb/sq ft above the bottom; 150 sq ft x 0.5 = 75 lb; 75 / 50 = 1.5, rounded up to two 50-lb bags (bag size: motz-bag-sizes). The 150 sq ft path is illustrative, not a measured yard.

fact: Shaw's ShawGrass installation guidelines finish sand infill with 1/2 to 3/4 inch of blade showing, warn that too much exposed fiber (not enough infill) lets the fibers mat or crush under heavy foot traffic and wear early, and put a 50- to 80-ounce turf at typically 4 pounds of infill per square foot, up to 5 for heavier products.
quote: Repeat the infill spread/ fiber brooming process until the infill is evenly spread such that no less than ½” - ¾” of turf fiber tips are exposed above the level of the infill. … F. CAUTION: Too much fiber exposed (not enough infill) will cause the fibers to mat or crush with heavy foot traffic. This will lead to premature wearing of the fiber … I. For a 50-to-80 ounce product, typically four pounds per square foot will be used. Heavier products may use up to five pounds per square foot.
source_label: Shaw Industries, ShawGrass Installation Guidelines (PDF), step 7, Infill Installation
notes: "pro-cess" is hyphenated across a line break in the PDF. The same step goes on to say too little infill voids the maker's coverage; the page does not repeat that. Footer code 021516; PDF metadata dates it February 2016.

fact: The Synthetic Turf Council's maintenance guidelines say infill settles into new turf over several months of use and rain, after which depth should be checked for consistency; that high-use areas lose more infill and edges collect it; that replacement infill should meet the builder's specification; and that a depth gauge or a nail and tape measure on a grid is the preferred way to measure.
quote: Expectation—After a period of several months of initial use of the field and rainfall, the infill material will settle into the synthetic turf. During this period, more frequent brushing may be advised by your field builder. Once settling occurs, check the infill depth for consistency around the field and to ensure it is within the field builder’s guidelines. … High use areas are prone to greater infill displacement. … Infill may accumulate at the edges of a field. If so, clean the material prior to brushing back into the main field. Replacement infill should meet the field builder’s specifications. Using an infill depth gauge or a nail and tape measure on a grid pattern is the preferred way to measure infill depth and consistency.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)
notes: Written for sports fields; the page applies the principles to a yard and says so.

fact: The same guidelines advise checking infill levels after heavy rain in case it has migrated down the slope, and say a blower should not be pointed straight into the turf and should run at minimal throttle to limit infill movement.
quote: After heavy rainfall, it is advisable to check the infill levels in case of migration with the field slope. … To minimize or eliminate the movement of infill, do not point nozzle directly into the turf. Use minimal throttle to decrease the volume of air.
source_label: Synthetic Turf Council, Guidelines for Maintenance of Infilled Synthetic Turf Systems (January 2013, Rev. 1)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape, a turf maker, says infill is displaced from high-traffic areas and washed out by heavy rain, that parting the blades with your fingers should show infill clearly covering the backing, and that a top-up should use the same type of infill originally installed, spread thin and brushed down to the base of the fibers.
quote: Checking Infill Levels: Over time, infill can get displaced from high-traffic areas or wash out from heavy rains. You can check the levels by parting the grass fibers with your fingers. You should see the infill clearly covering the backing. Topping Up Infill: If levels are low, you can add more. Purchase the same type of infill that was originally installed. Use a drop spreader to apply a thin layer over the area, then use your broom to work it down into the base of the fibers.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (Nov. 27, 2025)

fact: FieldTurf Landscape warns that a leaf blower's high air pressure can displace or remove infill and advises a low setting and a safe distance, and says a pressure washer should stay below 1500 PSI and spray at an angle, not straight down, to avoid displacing infill.
quote: However, it should be used with caution, as high air pressure can displace or remove the infill. Opt for a low-power setting, keep the blower at a safe distance from the turf, and use gentle sweeping motions to avoid disturbing the infill. … Keep the pressure setting below 1500 PSI. Always spray at an angle, not straight down, to avoid displacing the turf infill.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (Nov. 27, 2025)

fact: Firestone's code requires artificial turf to be maintained to mimic healthy living turf, cleaned and groomed to keep its appearance, and repaired or replaced where damaged or worn so that it matches the existing turf.
quote: i. Artificial turf shall be maintained in a manner to mimic healthy living turf. ii. Artificial turf shall be cleaned as necessary and groomed to maintain its appearance. … Damaged or worn areas shall be repaired or removed and replaced in manner that results in consistent appearance with the existing artificial turf.
source_label: Firestone Development Code 16.6.4.F.2.f (codified through Ord. No. 1072, Dec. 10, 2025)
notes: Read 2026-09-25 through the Municode content API (jobId 488870, productId 18062) for the same node. Item iii (depressions, excessive wear, odors) is dog-turf-infill.firestone-no-odors; item v (infill material) is dog-turf-infill.firestone-infill-antimicrobial.

fact: The Colorado Climate Center says chinook winds, warmed as they descend to the plains, bring large and sudden temperature rises, with jumps of 25 to 35°F in a short time not uncommon.
quote: Occasionally, when the plains are covered with a shallow layer of cold air, strong westerly winds aloft work their way to the surface. Warmed by rapid descent from higher levels, these winds bring large and sudden temperature rises. This phenomenon is the "chinook;" of the high plains and temperature rises of 25 to 35°F within a short time are not uncommon.
source_label: Colorado Climate Center (Colorado State University), Climate of Colorado
notes: The source prints "chinook;" with the semicolon inside the quotation marks. The page links chinook melt to runoff across the turf as its own inference, not the Climate Center's.

fact: Motz says old infill comes out with a vacuum before new infill goes in, and that the vacuum should be one made for artificial turf or a wet/dry shop vacuum, never a household vacuum; the turf itself stays unless it is in poor condition.
quote: To replace your infill and install Envirofill, you must first remove your previous infill by using a vacuum to suck the old infill out of the turf. … When vacuuming your artificial turf infill, do not use a household vacuum. Use one designed for artificial turf or a wet/dry vacuum (shop vac). Your turf itself does not need to be removed unless it is in poor condition and ready for a replacement.
source_label: The Motz Group, Synthetic Turf Infill FAQ

fact: FieldTurf Landscape says the amount and condition of a putting green's infill directly affect how the ball rolls, and that a green needs regular brushing and may need topping off to keep its speed.
quote: Infill Management for Ball Speed: The amount and condition of the infill directly impact how the ball rolls. Your installer can provide specific guidance, but generally, you’ll need to brush the green regularly to keep the infill evenly distributed and may need to top it off to maintain the desired speed.
source_label: FieldTurf Landscape, Artificial Turf Maintenance Guide (Nov. 27, 2025)
